authoritativeSources.title: NIST SP 800-190: Application Container Security Guide
authoritativeSources.summary: NIST SP 800-190 Executive Summary: "Use container-specific host OSs instead of general-purpose ones to reduce attack surfaces. A container-specific host OS is a minimalist OS explicitly designed to only run containers, with all other services and functionality disabled, and with read-only file systems and other hardening practices employed." §4.1.1: "Adopt container-specific vulnerability management tools and processes for images to prevent compromises. Traditional vulnerability management tools make many assumptions about host durability and app update mechanisms that are fundamentally misaligned with a containerized model." §4.3.4: "Only group containers with the same purpose, sensitivity, and threat posture on a single host OS kernel to allow for additional defense in depth." §4.4.3: "Containers should be run with their root filesystems in read-only mode. This approach isolates writes to specifically defined directories." §4.3.1: "Use separate namespaces for production and non-production workloads."

configExamples.title: Pod Security Standards - Restricted Profile (§4.4)
configExamples.code:
# NIST SP 800-190 §4.4: "Use container-aware runtime defense tools...
# capable of preventing, detecting, and responding to threats."
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: production
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted

configExamples.title: Security Context - Non-Root Container (§4.4.3)
configExamples.code:
# NIST SP 800-190 §4.4.3: "Containers should be run with their root
# filesystems in read-only mode... run as a non-root user."
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secure-pod
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    fsGroup: 2000
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:latest
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop:
          - ALL

configExamples.title: Container Image Scanning Policy (§4.1)
configExamples.code:
# NIST SP 800-190 §4.1: "Adopt container-specific vulnerability management
# tools and processes for images to prevent compromises."
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: admission-policy
data:
  policy.yaml: |
    apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
    kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
    spec:
      failurePolicy: Fail
      matchConstraints:
        resourceRules:
        - apiGroups: [""]
          resources: ["pods"]
          operations: ["CREATE"]
      validations:
      - expression: "object.spec.containers.all(c, !c.image.contains(':latest'))"
        message: "Images must use specific version tags, not :latest"

configExamples.title: BAD: hostPath Volume Mount (AVOID)
configExamples.code:
# BAD: hostPath volumes expose host filesystem to containers
# Per K8s Pod Security Standards: "HostPath volumes must be forbidden"
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: dangerous-host-mount
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:latest
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /host-data
      name: host-volume
  volumes:
  - name: host-volume
    hostPath:
      path: /var/run/docker.sock  # CRITICAL: Container escape vector!
      type: Socket

# Why this is dangerous:
# - Access to docker.sock allows creating privileged containers
# - Can read/write any file on the host
# - Common attack path: mount /, read /etc/shadow, write SSH keys
# - Fails both Baseline and Restricted Pod Security Standards

# Instead use: persistentVolumeClaim, configMap, secret, emptyDir

configExamples.title: BAD: Host Namespace Sharing (AVOID)
configExamples.code:
# BAD: Sharing host namespaces breaks container isolation
# Per K8s Pod Security Standards: "Sharing the host namespaces must be disallowed"
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: dangerous-host-namespaces
spec:
  hostNetwork: true  # BAD: Can sniff all host network traffic
  hostPID: true      # BAD: Can see/signal all host processes
  hostIPC: true      # BAD: Can access host shared memory
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:latest
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
      hostPort: 80   # BAD: Binds directly to host port

# Risks:
# - hostNetwork: Container can impersonate host services, MITM attacks
# - hostPID: Can kill/trace other processes, read /proc secrets
# - hostIPC: Can read shared memory from other processes
# - hostPort: Port conflicts, bypasses service abstractions

# These all fail the Baseline Pod Security Standard

configExamples.title: GOOD: Restricted Pod Security Context
configExamples.code:
# GOOD: Pod meeting Restricted security standard
# Per K8s docs: "Following current Pod hardening best practices"
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secure-restricted-pod
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 65534  # nobody user
    fsGroup: 65534
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault  # Required for Restricted
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp@sha256:abc123...  # Use digest, not tag
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # Required for Restricted
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop:
          - ALL               # Required: Drop all capabilities
        add:
          - NET_BIND_SERVICE  # Only allowed capability to add back
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 128Mi
      requests:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 64Mi
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}  # Allowed volume type in Restricted

authoritativeSources.title: SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria: Boundary Defense (CC6.6)
authoritativeSources.summary: SOC 2 CC6.6: "The entity implements logical access security measures to protect against threats from sources outside its system boundaries." Boundary Defense unifies digital controls by securing network perimeters with encryption, firewalls, and segmentation. Kubernetes Network Policies and service mesh implementations directly support CC6.6 requirements for restricting and monitoring traffic between trusted and untrusted connections. Source: AICPA Trust Services Criteria.

authoritativeSources.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.22 - Segregation of Networks
authoritativeSources.summary: ISO 27001:2022 A.8.22: "Groups of information services, users and information systems shall be segregated in networks." Control 8.22 enables organisations to segregate their computing networks into sub-networks based on the level of sensitivity and criticality and restrict the flow of traffic between these different sub-networks. Kubernetes namespaces and NetworkPolicies implement network segregation aligned with ISO 27001 requirements. Source: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A.

authoritativeSources.title: CSA Cloud Controls Matrix v4: Infrastructure & Virtualization Security (IVS)
authoritativeSources.summary: CCM IVS-06: "Network environments and virtual instances shall be designed and configured to restrict and monitor traffic between trusted and untrusted connections." CCM IVS-08: "Production and non-production environments shall be separated to prevent unauthorized access or changes to information assets." CCM IVS-09: "Multi-tenant applications and infrastructure shall be designed such that provider and customer user access is appropriately segmented from other tenant users." Kubernetes implements these CCM controls through namespaces, NetworkPolicies, and RBAC. Source: CSA Cloud Controls Matrix v4.0.

configExamples.title: GOOD: Rootless Docker Configuration

# Docker Rootless Mode - eliminates root privilege requirement
# "Rootless mode executes the Docker daemon and containers inside
# a user namespace. This is very useful to mitigate potential
# container-breakout vulnerabilities."

# Install rootless Docker
dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install

# Set environment variables
export PATH=/home/$USER/bin:$PATH
export DOCKER_HOST=unix:///run/user/$(id -u)/docker.sock

# Enable Docker Content Trust for image verification
# "When DCT is enabled, images must be signed by a trusted
# publisher before they can be pulled or run."
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1

# Sign and push an image
docker trust sign myregistry/myapp:v1.0.0

# View image signatures
docker trust inspect --pretty myregistry/myapp:v1.0.0

configExamples.title: GOOD: Capability Dropping Best Practice
configExamples.code:
# Linux Capabilities - principle of least privilege
# "By default, Docker drops all capabilities except those needed"
# but you should explicitly drop ALL and add only what's required.

# View default container capabilities
docker run --rm alpine sh -c 'cat /proc/1/status | grep Cap'

# Run with minimal capabilities (recommended)
docker run -d \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --cap-add CHOWN \
  --cap-add SETGID \
  --cap-add SETUID \
  --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  nginx:alpine

# Common capabilities and their uses:
# NET_BIND_SERVICE - Bind to ports below 1024
# CHOWN            - Change file ownership
# SETGID/SETUID    - Change process GID/UID
# DAC_OVERRIDE     - Bypass file permission checks (AVOID)
# SYS_ADMIN        - Many admin operations (AVOID - too broad)

configExamples.title: BAD vs GOOD: Network Isolation
configExamples.code:
# BAD: Container with host network (no isolation)
docker run -d \
  --network host \      # INSECURE: Shares host network namespace
  --name exposed-app \
  myapp:latest

# GOOD: Container with isolated bridge network
docker network create --driver bridge \
  --subnet=172.18.0.0/16 \
  --opt com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false \
  isolated-net

docker run -d \
  --network isolated-net \
  --publish 8080:80 \   # Only expose required ports
  --name secure-app \
  myapp:latest

# GOOD: Disable inter-container communication
# In daemon.json: "icc": false

Access to such APIs should require authentication tokens that have either been digitally signed or is verified with an authoritative source."

authoritativeSources.title: NIST SP 800-204B: Attribute-based Access Control for Microservices
authoritativeSources.summary: NIST SP 800-204B §1: "With the disappearance of a network perimeter because of the need to provide ubiquitous access to applications from multiple remote locations using different types of devices, it is necessary to build the concept of zero trust into the application environment." §4.6.6 APE-SR-3: "A default policy should be authored in the system that rejects all requests that are unauthenticated, mandates that service and end-user credentials be present on every request, restricts all communication to services within the application's own namespace." ISMC-SR-1: "The signing certificate used by the service mesh's CA module should be rooted in the organization's existing Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)."

configExamples.title: RequestAuthentication - End-User JWT (EAUN-SR-1)
configExamples.code:
# NIST SP 800-204B §4.4.3 EAUN-SR-1: "A request authentication policy
# must, at the minimum, provide instructions for extracting the credential
# from the request and instructions for validating the credential."
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata:
  name: jwt-auth
  namespace: production
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:

  jwtRules:

configExamples.title: AuthorizationPolicy - ABAC with Claims (EUAZ-SR-3)
configExamples.code:
# NIST SP 800-204B §4.5.2 EUAZ-SR-3: "All application traffic should
# carry end user credentials, and there should be a policy in the mesh
# enforcing that credentials are present."
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-jwt-claims
  namespace: production
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        requestPrincipals: ["https://auth.example.com/*"]
    when:
    - key: request.auth.claims[groups]
      values: ["admin", "developers"]

configExamples.title: AuthorizationPolicy - Service-Level (SAUZ-SR-1)

# NIST SP 800-204B §4.5.1 SAUZ-SR-1: "A policy object describing
# service-to-service access should be in place for all services in the mesh.
# Policies should describe the minimum access required for application
# functionality."

    - operation:
        methods: ["GET"]
        paths: ["/info*"]
    - operation:
        methods: ["POST"]
        paths: ["/data"]

configExamples.title: BAD: Permissive mTLS Mode (AVOID)
configExamples.code:
# BAD: Permissive mode accepts both mTLS and plaintext traffic
# Per Istio docs: "it also weakens the security stance"
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1

  name: default
  namespace: istio-system

  namespace: istio-system

configExamples.source: Istio Security Best Practices - Mutual TLS

configExamples.title: GOOD: Default-Deny Authorization Pattern
configExamples.code:
# Per Istio docs: "We recommend you define your Istio authorization
# policies following the default-deny pattern to enhance your
# cluster's security posture."
---
# Step 1: Deny all traffic by default
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-nothing
  namespace: production
spec:
  {}  # Empty spec denies all

---
# Step 2: Explicitly allow required traffic
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-backend
  namespace: production
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/production/sa/frontend"]
    to:
    - operation:
        paths: ["/api/*"]
configExamples.source: Istio Security Best Practices - Default-Deny Pattern

configExamples.title: BAD: Overly Broad Gateway Hosts (AVOID)
configExamples.code:
# BAD: Allows any VirtualService to bind, exposing unexpected domains
# "Avoid overly broad hosts settings in Gateway"
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: insecure-gateway
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
    hosts:
    - "*"  # INSECURE - any domain can bind

# GOOD: Lock down to specific domains/namespaces
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: secure-gateway
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
    tls:
      mode: SIMPLE
      credentialName: tls-secret
    hosts:
    - "api.example.com"           # Specific domain only
    - "default/app.example.com"   # Only default namespace
configExamples.source: Istio Security Best Practices - Gateway Security

configExamples.title: GOOD: Path Normalization for Security
configExamples.code:
# Enable strict path normalization to prevent bypass attacks
# "The safest choice is the strictest normalization option"
apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: IstioOperator
spec:
  meshConfig:
    pathNormalization:
      normalization: DECODE_AND_MERGE_SLASHES
    # Options:
    # - NONE: No normalization (risky)
    # - BASE: RFC 3986 normalization (default)
    # - MERGE_SLASHES: Merge duplicate slashes
    # - DECODE_AND_MERGE_SLASHES: Most secure option

# Apply via istioctl:
# istioctl upgrade --set meshConfig.pathNormalization.normalization=DECODE_AND_MERGE_SLASHES
configExamples.source: Istio Security Best Practices - Path Normalization

configExamples.title: GOOD: Limit Downstream Connections
configExamples.code:
# Prevent resource exhaustion attacks (CVE-2020-007)
# "By default, Istio has no limit on downstream connections"
apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: IstioOperator
spec:
  meshConfig:
    defaultConfig:
      runtimeValues:
        "overload.global_downstream_max_connections": "100000"
configExamples.source: Istio Security Best Practices - Connection Limits

configExamples.title: BAD: No AuthorizationPolicy (Default Allow-All)
configExamples.code:
# BAD: Without AuthorizationPolicy, ALL traffic is allowed by default
# Per Istio docs: "If no authorization policies apply to a workload,
# Istio allows all requests to that workload."
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: production
  labels:
    istio-injection: enabled
# MISSING: AuthorizationPolicy resources!
# ANY service can call ANY other service - no access control

# Risk: Lateral movement after initial compromise is unrestricted
# Risk: No enforcement of least-privilege between services

configExamples.title: BAD: ALLOW_ANY Outbound Traffic (AVOID)
configExamples.code:
# BAD: ALLOW_ANY permits workloads to call any external service
# Per NIST SP 800-204A SM-DR9: "The service mesh should be capable of
# disabling communication to any service outside the cluster."
apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: IstioOperator
spec:
  meshConfig:
    outboundTrafficPolicy:
      mode: ALLOW_ANY  # INSECURE - no egress control!

# Risks:
# - Data exfiltration to arbitrary external endpoints
# - C2 communication from compromised workloads
# - Supply chain attacks via malicious dependencies

# GOOD: Use REGISTRY_ONLY to restrict egress
# mode: REGISTRY_ONLY  # Only allow registered ServiceEntries
configExamples.source: NIST SP 800-204A SM-DR9 - Outbound Traffic Control

configExamples.title: BAD: No Path Normalization (AVOID)
configExamples.code:
# BAD: Without path normalization, authorization can be bypassed
# Attack: /api/admin%2F../public may bypass "/api/admin/*" rule
# Per Istio docs: "The safest choice is the strictest normalization option"
apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: IstioOperator
spec:
  meshConfig:
    pathNormalization:
      normalization: NONE  # INSECURE - path traversal attacks possible!

# Common bypass patterns:
# - /path/../secret -> /secret
# - /path%2F..%2Fsecret -> may bypass
# - //path -> /path (double slash)

# GOOD: Use DECODE_AND_MERGE_SLASHES for maximum protection
configExamples.source: Istio Security Best Practices - Path Normalization

configExamples.title: BAD: JWT Without Audience Validation (AVOID)
configExamples.code:
# BAD: JWT validation without audience check allows token reuse attacks
# Per RFC 7519: "The audience claim identifies the recipients that
# the JWT is intended for."
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata:
  name: weak-jwt-auth
  namespace: production
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  jwtRules:
  - issuer: "https://auth.example.com"
    jwksUri: "https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json"
    # MISSING: audiences field!
    # Token issued for service-A can be replayed to service-B

# GOOD: Always specify expected audience
# jwtRules:
# - issuer: "https://auth.example.com"
#   jwksUri: "https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json"
#   audiences: ["api.example.com"]  # Validate intended recipient
configExamples.source: Istio Security Best Practices - JWT Validation

    config.linkerd.io/skip-outbound-ports: "5432"

configExamples.title: GOOD: Production-Ready Secure Installation
configExamples.code:
# GOOD: Proper production Linkerd installation with long-lived certs

# 1. Generate trust anchor (10 years)
step certificate create root.linkerd.cluster.local ca.crt ca.key \
  --profile root-ca --no-password --insecure --not-after 87600h

# 2. Generate issuer certificate (1 year, auto-rotate with cert-manager)
step certificate create identity.linkerd.cluster.local issuer.crt issuer.key \
  --profile intermediate-ca --not-after 8760h --no-password --insecure \
  --ca ca.crt --ca-key ca.key

# 3. Install with HA mode (required for policy enforcement)
# Per Linkerd docs: "If policy is a strict requirement, you should pair
# the usage of these features with HA mode"
linkerd install \
  --identity-trust-anchors-file ca.crt \
  --identity-issuer-certificate-file issuer.crt \
  --identity-issuer-key-file issuer.key \
  --identity-issuance-lifetime=24h \
  --ha \
  | kubectl apply -f -

# 4. Set cluster-wide default deny
kubectl annotate ns --all \
  config.linkerd.io/default-inbound-policy=cluster-authenticated

configExamples.title: GOOD: Enforce Severity Threshold with Audit Trail
configExamples.code:
# GOOD: Properly configured CI/CD security gate
name: Secure Build Pipeline
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  security-scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Run Snyk Security Scan
        uses: snyk/actions/node@master
        env:
          SNYK_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SNYK_TOKEN }}
        with:
          # Fail on high/critical vulnerabilities
          args: >-
            --severity-threshold=high
            --fail-on=all
            --all-projects
            --detection-depth=4

      - name: Upload SARIF results
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        if: always()  # Upload even on failure for audit
        with:
          sarif_file: snyk.sarif

      - name: Generate SBOM for compliance
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'

guides.name: Amazon Bedrock
guides.description: Fully managed foundation model platform with a unified API, agents, knowledge bases, and guardrails

authoritativeSources.title: What is Amazon Bedrock?
authoritativeSources.summary: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that provides foundation models from leading AI companies and Amazon through a unified API. It supports building generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI capabilities, including model evaluation, RAG with knowledge bases, agents, and guardrails. Bedrock offers a serverless experience for experimentation, customization, and deployment without managing infrastructure.

authoritativeSources.title: Security in Amazon Bedrock
authoritativeSources.summary: Amazon Bedrock follows the AWS shared responsibility model, outlining security of the cloud vs. security in the cloud. The security guidance covers data protection, IAM configuration, incident response, resilience, and monitoring topics for Bedrock workloads.

configExamples.title: Least-privilege IAM policy — scope to specific model ARN
configExamples.source: AWS Docs — Identity-based policy examples for Amazon Bedrock
configExamples.discussion: By explicitly denying bedrock:* and then allowing only the specific InvokeModel actions on a single model ARN, you prevent accidental access to other Bedrock APIs (CreateModelCustomizationJob, DeleteGuardrail, etc.) and restrict inference to the approved model.

configExamples.title: SCP — deny inference on unapproved models
configExamples.source: AWS Docs — Condition keys for Amazon Bedrock
configExamples.discussion: Service Control Policies (SCPs) at the AWS Organizations level override any identity-based Allow. Use bedrock:FoundationModelIdentifier to restrict which foundation models can be invoked across all accounts in an OU.

configExamples.title: IAM policy — allow provisioned throughput invocation only
configExamples.source: AWS Docs — Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
configExamples.discussion: Restricting invocations to provisioned-model ARNs ensures that all inference goes through reserved capacity. The explicit Deny on foundation-model ARNs prevents fallback to on-demand billing.

configExamples.title: Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch and S3
configExamples.discussion: Model invocation logging captures prompt inputs and model outputs for audit and compliance. Enable textDataDeliveryEnabled to log prompt/completion text. Use both CloudWatch (real-time monitoring) and S3 (long-term retention) destinations.

configExamples.title: Create VPC endpoint for private Bedrock access
configExamples.code:
# Create an interface VPC endpoint for Bedrock Runtime so inference
# traffic stays on the AWS private network (no internet traversal).

aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.bedrock-runtime \
  --subnet-ids subnet-0123456789abcdef0 subnet-abcdef0123456789a \
  --security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --private-dns-enabled

# Also create an endpoint for the Bedrock control plane if needed:
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.bedrock \
  --subnet-ids subnet-0123456789abcdef0 subnet-abcdef0123456789a \
  --security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --private-dns-enabled
configExamples.source: AWS Docs — Use Amazon Bedrock with an interface VPC endpoint
configExamples.discussion: Interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) keep Bedrock API traffic within the VPC. Create separate endpoints for bedrock (control plane) and bedrock-runtime (inference). Enable --private-dns-enabled so the standard bedrock-runtime.REGION.amazonaws.com hostname resolves to the endpoint ENIs.

authoritativeSources.title: Does Amazon Bedrock share data with model providers or use it for training?
authoritativeSources.summary: Amazon Bedrock does not store customer input or output data, share data with third-party model providers, or use it to train models. Model invocations stay within the AWS network using dedicated deployment accounts that model providers cannot access.

authoritativeSources.title: Generative AI with Amazon Bedrock — Network Architecture & Data Flow (Ch. 12)
authoritativeSources.summary: Kwatra & Kaushik (Packt, 2024) detail Bedrock's on-demand, provisioned-throughput, and model-customization network architectures. Each model provider gets a dedicated deployment account per region that customers and other vendors cannot access. All internal traffic uses TLS 1.2+, no customer data is persisted in the Bedrock service account, and model providers never see customer prompts, outputs, or training data — even for Amazon's own Titan models.

authoritativeSources.title: Generative AI with Amazon Bedrock — KMS Encryption for Bedrock Resources (Ch. 12)
authoritativeSources.summary: Kwatra & Kaushik (Packt, 2024) cover encrypting Bedrock resources with customer-managed KMS keys across four areas: knowledge-base transient data and vector stores, model customization jobs (with separate builder/user IAM roles), agent resources using encryption context conditions, and guardrails. Each resource type has distinct KMS policy requirements; the chapter provides IAM policy examples for granting Bedrock the necessary Decrypt, GenerateDataKey, and CreateGrant permissions.

authoritativeSources.title: Generative AI with Amazon Bedrock — IAM Governance & Least Privilege (Ch. 12)
authoritativeSources.summary: Kwatra & Kaushik (Packt, 2024) present an IAM governance checklist for Bedrock: audit access patterns with CloudTrail and IAM Access Analyzer, implement ABAC using resource tags (e.g., Env:Dev), enforce permissions boundaries, restrict models via SCPs at the Organizations level, establish user lifecycle policies to prevent permissions creep, and build a job-role matrix mapping roles to Bedrock actions like InvokeModel and ListFoundationModels.

authoritativeSources.title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
authoritativeSources.summary: Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable safety and privacy safeguards across models. It supports content filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters, and grounding checks to help reduce harmful or irrelevant outputs in applications.

configExamples.title: Create guardrail with content filters and PII detection
configExamples.discussion: Content filters evaluate input/output against built-in categories with configurable strength levels (NONE, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH). PII filters detect and either ANONYMIZE (replace with placeholder) or BLOCK the response entirely. Set PROMPT_ATTACK outputStrength to NONE since it only applies to inputs.

configExamples.title: SCP — require guardrail on every InvokeModel call
configExamples.source: AWS Docs — Amazon Bedrock condition keys
configExamples.discussion: By checking the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key, this SCP ensures that every model invocation in the organization includes a guardrail. Calls without a guardrail ARN are denied. Combine with the account-level guardrail enforcement API for defense in depth.

authoritativeSources.title: Generative AI with Amazon Bedrock — Ethical Practices & Responsible AI (Ch. 12)
authoritativeSources.summary: Kwatra & Kaushik (Packt, 2024) address three categories of ethical risk in Bedrock workloads: veracity (hallucinations mitigated via prompt engineering, RAG, and temperature tuning), intellectual property (training-data provenance, content filtering, and watermarking), and safety/toxicity (guardrails, data curation, and responsible AI policies). The authors recommend combining Bedrock Guardrails with organizational responsible-AI governance frameworks.

authoritativeSources.title: Amazon Bedrock Agents
authoritativeSources.summary: Bedrock Agents orchestrate foundation models, knowledge bases, and action groups to automate multi-step tasks. Agents can collect information, invoke APIs, and use knowledge bases while Bedrock manages prompting, memory, monitoring, and permissions.

authoritativeSources.title: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
authoritativeSources.summary: Knowledge Bases enable RAG workflows by connecting proprietary data sources to Bedrock. They retrieve relevant data, can provide citations, support multimodal inputs, and keep content in sync with connected data sources.

authoritativeSources.title: AWS CLI Command Reference: Bedrock
authoritativeSources.summary: AWS CLI references for all Bedrock service namespaces: control-plane operations (models, guardrails, customization, logging), agent management (agents, action groups, prompts, knowledge bases), agent runtime (invoke agents, sessions, KB queries), and inference runtime (invoke models, apply guardrails, async invocations).

authoritativeSources.title: AWS Bedrock Security Config Rules Pack
authoritativeSources.summary: 21 automated AWS Config security controls for Bedrock deployments covering wildcard permissions, guardrails enforcement, encryption, VPC endpoints, logging, and RAG knowledge base security. MIT-0 licensed.

configExamples.title: Deploy the Bedrock Config Rules Pack
configExamples.code:
# Clone the repo and deploy all 21 security controls via CloudFormation.
# The deploy script handles SSM parameters, S3 bucket creation, Lambda
# packaging, and stack deployment automatically.

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-bedrock-security-config-rules-pack.git
cd sample-bedrock-security-config-rules-pack

# Edit parameters/ssm-parameters.yaml to enable/disable specific controls,
# then deploy with a unique S3 bucket name for templates:
./scripts/deploy.sh --bucket my-bedrock-configrules-bucket

# Deploy to a specific region with an AWS profile:
./scripts/deploy.sh --bucket my-bedrock-configrules-bucket \
  --region us-west-2 --profile production
configExamples.discussion: The deploy script uses a two-stack architecture: an SSM parameters stack for configuration and a main CloudFormation stack for the Config rules. Only enabled controls are packaged and deployed, reducing the blast radius. Use --package-all to override and deploy everything.

configExamples.title: Selective control deployment via SSM parameters
configExamples.code:
# parameters/ssm-parameters.yaml — toggle individual controls on/off.
# Set Value to 'true' to deploy, 'false' to skip.

# Example: deploy only IAM, guardrails, and logging controls
DeployFMI01Param:          # Wildcard permissions check
  Type: AWS::SSM::Parameter
  Properties:
    Name: /bedrock-configrules/global/DeployFMI01
    Type: String
    Value: 'true'

DeployFMI02Param:          # Guardrails enforcement
  Type: AWS::SSM::Parameter
  Properties:
    Name: /bedrock-configrules/global/DeployFMI02
    Type: String
    Value: 'true'

DeployFMI04Param:          # Model invocation logging
  Type: AWS::SSM::Parameter
  Properties:
    Name: /bedrock-configrules/global/DeployFMI04
    Type: String
    Value: 'true'

DeployFMI09Param:          # VPC endpoint check
  Type: AWS::SSM::Parameter
  Properties:
    Name: /bedrock-configrules/global/DeployFMI09
    Type: String
    Value: 'false'

# Global settings
EnableAutoRemediationParam:
  Type: AWS::SSM::Parameter
  Properties:
    Name: /bedrock-configrules/global/EnableAutoRemediation
    Type: String
    Value: 'false'
configExamples.discussion: Each control has a Deploy* SSM parameter. Setting it to false causes the deploy script to skip packaging and deploying that control. The EnableAutoRemediation parameter controls whether non-compliant resources are automatically remediated. Start with false and enable after testing.

configExamples.title: Check compliance status for a Bedrock Config rule
configExamples.code:
# List all Bedrock security Config rules
aws configservice describe-config-rules \
  --query "ConfigRules[?starts_with(ConfigRuleName, 'bedrock-security')].ConfigRuleName" \
  --output table

# Get compliance details for the wildcard permissions rule
aws configservice get-compliance-details-by-config-rule \
  --config-rule-name bedrock-security-fmi-01-wildcard-permissions \
  --compliance-types NON_COMPLIANT \
  --query "EvaluationResults[].{Resource:EvaluationResultIdentifier.EvaluationResultQualifier.ResourceId,Status:ComplianceType,Annotation:Annotation}" \
  --output table

# Get overall compliance summary across all Bedrock rules
aws configservice describe-compliance-by-config-rule \
  --config-rule-names \
    bedrock-security-fmi-01-wildcard-permissions \
    bedrock-security-fmi-02-guardrails-enforced \
    bedrock-security-fmi-04-invocation-logging \
  --output table
configExamples.discussion: After deploying the Config rules pack, use these commands to monitor compliance posture. NON_COMPLIANT results include an Annotation field explaining the specific violation (e.g., which role has wildcard bedrock:* permissions). Integrate with AWS Security Hub for centralized compliance dashboards.

authoritativeSources.title: AWS IAM Privilege Escalation — iam:PassRole + Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter
